note: The datasheet library: every source of data the explainer computes from or quotes, and sources worth adding. Status is not stored here; src/scripts/library.js works it out from usedBy at build time. A use without `pr` must be cited (its `find` text present) in that file on this tree, or `npm run check` fails. `reuse` is what the source states about copying (open, cite, unknown); `licence` gives the detail, read on the `checked` date. Links only: no PDFs are rehosted.

sources.title: CIE 1931 colour-matching functions, 2 degree observer
sources.edition: data set from CIE 018:2019, Table 6; DOI 10.25039/CIE.DS.xvudnb9b
sources.provides: The standard observer at 1 nm: how strongly the eye's three colour channels respond to each wavelength. Every colour on the site is an integral against these curves.
sources.licence: CIE publishes its data sets under CC BY-SA 4.0 (read from the CIE D65 data set's metadata; share-alike means derived tables carry the same licence).

sources.title: Simple Analytic Approximations to the CIE XYZ Color Matching Functions
sources.by: Chris Wyman, Peter-Pike Sloan and Peter Shirley
sources.provides: A sum of piecewise Gaussians that reproduces the CIE 1931 curves to about 1%, so the engine needs no table.
sources.licence: Authors keep copyright; JCGT articles may be redistributed unmodified under CC BY-ND 4.0 and their code is under an open-source licence. The fit's coefficients are copied into optics-core.js with this citation.

sources.title: CIE standard illuminant D65, illuminant A, typical fluorescent lamps (FL11) and typical LED lamps (LED-B3)
sources.provides: Spectral power of daylight, tungsten, a tri-phosphor tube and a white LED, the lamps on the lamp switch. D65 doi 10.25039/CIE.DS.hjfjmt59; FLs 10.25039/CIE.DS.ukaymjdn; LEDs 10.25039/CIE.DS.vgssnyfg.
sources.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (stated in the D65 data set's metadata). The tables in lamps.json are copies, so they carry CC BY-SA.

sources.title: Colour (colour-science)
sources.provides: A Python colour-science library whose copies of the CIE tables were used to build lamps.json.
sources.licence: BSD 3-Clause.

sources.title: Optical spectroscopic study of tetrahedrally coordinated Co²⁺ in natural spinel and staurolite at different temperatures and pressures
sources.provides: Measured absorption of tetrahedral Co²⁺, the triplet that makes cobalt blue. The page takes the band's shape from it and places the centres for silicate glass by estimate.
sources.licence: Journal article; no reuse licence stated (the PDF is restricted).

sources.title: Glasses for Protecting the Eyes from Injurious Radiations
sources.by: W. W. Coblentz and W. B. Emerson, Bureau of Standards
sources.edition: Technologic Paper 93; the free copy is the 3rd edition, 1919
sources.provides: Measured ultraviolet, visible and infrared transmission of protective glasses, including ferrous heat-absorbing glass. Sets the strength of the Fe²⁺ infrared band on the glory-hole lenses.
sources.licence: US government work; no licence stated on the document.

sources.title: The CIEDE2000 color-difference formula: implementation notes, supplementary test data, and mathematical observations
sources.by: Gaurav Sharma, Wencheng Wu and Edul N. Dalal
sources.provides: The colour-difference formula and test data the rack's recipe fits are scored with.
sources.licence: Journal article; formula used with citation.

sources.title: A Low-Dimensional Function Space for Efficient Spectral Upsampling
sources.provides: The three-number sigmoid spectrum used to relight photographed swatches under other lamps.
sources.licence: Journal article; method used with citation.

sources.title: Bullseye Glass Co. online store
sources.edition: swept for the rack (328 colours, COE 90)
sources.provides: Names, codes and product photos of Bullseye sheet, frit, rod and billet. Rack swatches are sampled from the photos; colorants are inferred from names.
sources.licence: No data licence stated. The repo keeps names, codes, links and one sampled colour per product, not the photos.

sources.title: Glass Alchemy online store
sources.provides: Names and product photos of Glass Alchemy borosilicate colour rod. Swatches sampled from photos.
sources.licence: No data licence stated. Names, links and sampled colours only.

sources.title: Frantz Art Glass online store
sources.by: Frantz Art Glass (a Perle di Vetro company)
sources.edition: swept for Effetre, Reichenbach, CiM, Vetrofond, Double Helix, Northstar and TAG
sources.provides: Catalogue codes, names and photos for seven lampwork rod brands a retailer resells. Swatches sampled from photos.
sources.licence: No data licence stated. Names, codes, links and sampled colours only.

sources.title: Craig Johnson's LED Museum: fluorescence spectra of a uranium glass marble
sources.provides: Spectrograph plots of a uranium glass marble fluorescing under a violet laser. The page places uranium glass's strongest emission peak near 527 nm from this site.
sources.licence: No copyright or terms notice on the page. Plots are images; no numbers are copied beyond the peak position.
sources.caution: uranium.js cites "spectrum 1001" under a 445 nm laser; the page found on 2026-10-19 is a uranium marble under a Blu-ray (about 405 nm) laser. The exact spectrum cited has not been re-found.

sources.title: Viscosity of a standard soda-lime-silica glass
sources.by: Albert Napolitano and Earl G. Hawkins, National Bureau of Standards
sources.provides: Viscosity of NBS Standard Glass No. 710 from 560 to 1400 °C, measured at eight laboratories, with a Fulcher fit and the strain (504 °C), annealing (546 °C) and softening (724 °C) points.
sources.licence: US government publication; no licence stated. Fit constants and fixed points are quoted with citation.

sources.title: ATS-129: Properties of Soda-Lime Silica Float Glass
sources.edition: technical bulletin, current edition dated 09/2026; PR #16 cites the 2013-01-14 edition
sources.provides: Elastic, thermal and optical constants of float glass: E = 72 GPa, expansion 8.3 × 10⁻⁶ /°C, density, conductivity, heat capacity, and a rule for reading stress from optical retardation.
sources.licence: Disclaimer only; no reuse licence stated.
sources.caution: The 2026 edition gives Poisson's ratio 0.22; the stage uses 0.23 from the 2013 edition.

sources.title: A Note on the Annealing of Optical Glass
sources.by: L. H. Adams and E. D. Williamson
sources.provides: Measurements of how stress decays in hot glass, the basis of annealing schedules.
sources.licence: Journal article; no reuse licence stated.

sources.title: Do cathedral glasses flow?
sources.provides: The shear modulus (about 30 GPa) and viscosity extrapolation that turn room-temperature glass into a relaxation time longer than the age of the universe.
sources.licence: Journal article (AIP); no reuse licence stated. PR #17 links an author-hosted PDF; the DOI is the record.

sources.title: Viscous flow of medieval cathedral glass
sources.by: Ozgur Gulbiten, John C. Mauro, Xiaoju Guo and Olus N. Boratav
sources.provides: Measured room-temperature viscosity of a medieval Westminster Abbey glass (10²⁴–10²⁵ Pa·s) and flow of about 1 nm per billion years.
sources.licence: Journal article (Wiley); no reuse licence stated.

sources.title: SCHOTT optical glass datasheets (N-BK7, F2, SF11, N-SF11)
sources.edition: values as in the SCHOTT Zemax catalogue 2017-01-20b; the downloads page gives no version for the current collection
sources.provides: Sellmeier coefficients, refractive index nd and Abbe number vd for each glass, plus internal transmittance and thermal data. The downloads page also offers the catalogue in Zemax format.
sources.licence: No terms of use on the downloads page. The repo takes the coefficients through the CC0 refractiveindex.info copy, and links SCHOTT for the datasheet itself.

sources.title: refractiveindex.info database
sources.provides: Optical constants of thousands of materials as YAML, including the SCHOTT, Ohara and Hoya catalogues. The source of every Sellmeier coefficient the site uses.
sources.licence: CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication).

sources.title: Interspecimen Comparison of the Refractive Index of Fused Silica
sources.provides: The standard Sellmeier fit for fused silica, 0.21 to 3.71 µm.
sources.licence: Journal article; coefficients quoted with citation.

sources.title: Optical properties of soda lime silica glasses
sources.provides: Refractive index and absorption of window glass from the ultraviolet to the infrared; the page's soda-lime index curve.
sources.licence: Journal article (Elsevier); coefficients quoted with citation.

sources.title: Council Directive 69/493/EEC on the approximation of the laws of the Member States relating to crystal glass
sources.provides: Legal definitions of lead crystal (at least 24% PbO) and full lead crystal (at least 30%), with density and refractive-index limits.
sources.licence: EU legislation; quoted with citation (EUR-Lex reuse terms not re-read).

sources.title: Authenticity screening of stained glass windows using optical spectroscopy
sources.by: Wendy Meulebroeck, Hilde Wouters, Karin Nys and Hugo Thienpont
sources.provides: Measured ultraviolet to near-infrared transmission of historical and modern coloured stained glass, with the absorption bands of cobalt, copper, iron, manganese and chromium identified.
sources.would: Real curves in place of the drawn ones for the common colorants, and an openly licensed set that can be copied into the repo.
sources.licence: CC BY 4.0.

sources.title: SCHOTT optical filter glass data sheets and calculation program
sources.edition: data sheets version June 2026 (169 pp); Excel calculation program with 2015 tutorial
sources.provides: Measured internal transmittance of coloured glasses, 200–5200 nm, at a reference thickness: cobalt blues (BG), coppers, ferrous heat absorbers (KG), selenium–cadmium long-pass reds and oranges (RG, OG), neutral densities (NG). The Excel tool rescales to any thickness.
sources.would: Industrial colored glass measured to datasheet standard, to check each drawn colorant curve and the Beer–Lambert thickness scaling against.
sources.licence: No reuse licence stated; values are "reference values". Use to check curves and quote individual numbers with citation, not to copy tables.

sources.title: SciGlass
sources.by: EPAM Systems (open release); SciGlass Next at Universität Jena
sources.edition: v1.0 MS Access release (May 2019), read through D. R. Cassar's plain-text conversion (github.com/drcassar/SciGlass, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.8287159); browsable as SciGlass Next at sciglass.uni-jena.de (API by key on request)
sources.provides: About 422,000 glass compositions with their properties (viscosity, transition temperature, expansion, index) and over 15,000 optical spectra, ultraviolet to near infrared. The bench uses 10,257 melts made only of its nine oxides, with measured viscosity points, index and Abbe number, extracted by tools/sciglass/extract.py.
sources.would: Measured spectra for uranium and didymium glass (the spectra are not in the open text conversion; SciGlass Next shows them).
sources.licence: ODbL per SciGlass Next; the GitHub LICENSE file is headed ODbL but its body is the MIT licence. Treat as ODbL (attribution and share-alike), the stricter reading: the extract public/data/sciglass/bench.json carries the ODbL notice and is offered under ODbL 1.0.
sources.caution: A compilation of literature values, not a curated reference: duplicates and mistyped entries exist (one entry at NBS 710's composition lists n = 1.618). Fluegel's viscosity model was fitted to much of the same literature, so agreement with it is a consistency check, not independent validation.

sources.title: TIE-29: Refractive Index and Dispersion
sources.provides: How SCHOTT defines and fits index: the Sellmeier form, Abbe numbers, partial dispersions and tolerances.
sources.would: A citable check on the cut stage's formulas and its Abbe-number definitions.
sources.licence: No reuse licence stated.

sources.title: TIE-35: Transmittance of optical glass
sources.edition: current PDF undated; earlier version October 2005
sources.provides: Internal versus external transmittance, surface reflection losses and how to rescale transmittance to another thickness.
sources.would: A source for the engine's two-surface reflection loss and thickness scaling, now stated without one.
sources.licence: No reuse licence stated.

sources.title: NIST Atomic Spectra Database (Standard Reference Database 78)
sources.by: A. Kramida, Yu. Ralchenko, J. Reader and the NIST ASD Team
sources.provides: Evaluated atomic lines. Sodium D2 588.995095 nm and D1 589.592424 nm in air, matching the values in flare.js.
sources.would: A citation for the sodium doublet the glory-hole stage uses, and lines for any other flame or lamp.
sources.licence: NIST Standard Reference Data can be copyrighted under the Standard Reference Data Act; no licence text found. Quote values with the recommended citation.

sources.title: Standard Reference Material 710a: Soda-Lime-Silica Glass
sources.by: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.provides: Certified viscosity from log η = 2 (1464 °C) to 5 (918 °C) poise and a certified softening point of 730.6 °C, with annealing 545 °C and strain 504 °C for information. A different melt from NBS 710 (zinc and alumina added).
sources.would: A second, certified soda-lime curve to show how much fixed points move between two similar glasses.
sources.licence: US government certificate; no licence stated.

sources.title: TechNotes 4: Heat & Glass, and the Annealing Thick Slabs chart
sources.provides: A studio glass maker's annealing soak (482 °C) and cooling rates by thickness, derived from Corning's method, and how kiln glass behaves at each temperature.
sources.would: Real studio schedules for the lehr, in place of float-glass numbers applied to studio glass.
sources.licence: © Bullseye Glass Co.; no reuse licence stated.

sources.title: Colour & Vision Research Laboratory database
sources.by: Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London
sources.provides: Tabulated colour-matching functions (CIE 1931, Stiles–Burch, CIE 2006), cone fundamentals and luminous efficiency.
sources.would: Tables to test the analytic observer against, and the CIE 2006 cone fundamentals if the page ever explains metamerism from the cones up.
sources.licence: "Provided free of charge as a service to the vision science community"; no explicit reuse licence.

sources.title: Glass viscosity calculation based on a global statistical modelling approach
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
sources.edition: Glass Technol.: Eur. J. Glass Sci. Technol. A 48(1), 13–30; author's copy on glassproperties.com
sources.provides: Isokom temperatures at 10^1.5, 10^6.6 and 10^12 Pa·s as polynomials in mol% composition, fitted to more than 2,200 silicate glasses (about 42–89 mol% SiO2), with the paper's own predictions for standard glasses (Table 12).
sources.licence: Journal article, author's copy; no reuse licence stated. Coefficients are quoted with citation.
sources.caution: Coefficients were read from the PDF by text extraction. Three were unreadable and are refitted to the paper's Table 12 (batch.json, viscosity.reconstructed); check them against Fluegel's spreadsheet when it can be fetched.

sources.title: Density and thermal expansion calculation of silicate glass melts from 1000 °C to 1400 °C
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, David A. Earl, Arun K. Varshneya and Thomas P. Seward III, Alfred University
sources.edition: Phys. Chem. Glasses: Eur. J. Glass Sci. Technol. B 49(5); author's copy on glassproperties.com
sources.provides: Melt density at 1000–1400 °C as a function of mol% composition (Table 2), fitted to SciGlass data for glasses above 40 mol% silica.
sources.licence: Journal article, author's copy; no reuse licence stated. Coefficients are quoted with citation.
sources.caution: A melt model. The bench scales its 1200 °C value to 2.50 g/cm³ for float glass, one contraction factor for every batch.

sources.title: Older thermal expansion models (Appen's factors, as tabulated)
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, after A. A. Appen, Glass Chemistry (1974)
sources.provides: Appen's additive factors for the linear expansion coefficient by mol%, including the composition-dependent rules for SiO2, B2O3, PbO and K2O. The page traces additive expansion factors back to Winkelmann and Schott (1894).
sources.licence: No terms stated on the site. Factors are quoted with citation.

sources.title: Effect of composition and other factors on the specific refraction and dispersion of glasses
sources.by: John C. Young and Alfred N. Finn, National Bureau of Standards
sources.provides: Specific refraction (n_D − 1)/ρ and specific dispersion (n_F − n_C)/ρ factors for each oxide, additive by weight.
sources.licence: US government publication; no licence stated. Factors are quoted with citation.

sources.title: Ferric-ferrous equilibria in natural silicate liquids at 1 bar
sources.by: Richard O. Sack, Ian S. E. Carmichael, Mark Rivers and Mark S. Ghiorso
sources.provides: ln(X_Fe2O3/X_FeO) as a function of oxygen fugacity, temperature and mole-fraction composition (Table 3).
sources.licence: Journal article; coefficients quoted with citation.
sources.caution: Fitted to natural lavas, with less alkali than soda-lime glass and no lead or boron.

sources.title: Glass compositions: typical commercial glasses
sources.provides: Typical compositions (mol%) of float, container, borosilicate and other commercial glasses.
sources.licence: No terms stated on the site. A few compositions are quoted with citation.
